name: Sending people to Mars
short_status: An aspiration with no programme behind it: as of 28 September 2026 we could find no funded human Mars programme, approved architecture or committed landing date anywhere. US space policy sets no Mars date, and its dated human exploration goals are all lunar.
stats: funded human Mars programmes we could find, September 2026
since the 1989 Space Exploration Initiative set a Mars goal
Starship flights to 28 September 2026; only the fourteenth reached orbit

facts.label: Current US policy
facts.value: Executive Order 14369, "Ensuring American Space Superiority", signed 18 December 2025 and published 23 December 2025. It sets two dated human exploration goals, both lunar: returning Americans to the Moon by 2028 through Artemis, and "establishing initial elements of a permanent lunar outpost by 2030". Mars appears exactly twice in the whole order, both times as justification, to "prepare for the journey to Mars" and "enable the next steps in Mars exploration". No Mars date is given anywhere in the order.

facts.label: The 2026 transport policy
facts.value: National Security Presidential Memorandum 17, "The National Space Transportation Policy", signed 20 August 2026 and published 25 August 2026, directs the NASA Administrator to "explore commercial robotic access to the surface of Mars" and to "explore commercial architectures for sending humans to the surface of Mars and returning them to Earth". It sets no Mars date and is to be carried out "subject to the availability of appropriations"; its only dated goal is that by 2030 US launch ranges must support more than 1,000 launches and reentries a year.

facts.label: The 1989 goal
facts.value: On 20 July 1989, the twentieth anniversary of Apollo 11, President George H. W. Bush proposed "Back to the Moon; back to the future. And this time, back to stay. And then a journey into tomorrow, a journey to another planet: a manned mission to Mars." He attached no date, asking the National Space Council to report back with "the necessary money, manpower, and materials" and "realistic timetables". Nothing flew from it.

facts.label: The 2010 goal
facts.value: At Kennedy Space Center on 15 April 2010, President Barack Obama said: "By the mid-2030s, I believe we can send humans to orbit Mars and return them safely to Earth. And a landing on Mars will follow." Sixteen years later there is no funded crewed mission to Mars orbit.

facts.label: The 2025 goal
facts.value: In his inaugural address on 20 January 2025, President Donald Trump said the United States "will pursue our manifest destiny into the stars, launching American astronauts to plant the Stars and Stripes on the planet Mars". No date or human Mars programme followed from that sentence. The administration's budget request of May 2025 proposed "$1 billion in new investments for Mars-focused programs", but we found no human Mars mission approved or funded since.

facts.label: SpaceX's plan as of May 2025
facts.value: In a presentation at Starbase in May 2025, Musk said "progress is measured by the timeline to establishing a self-sustaining civilization on Mars", and set out a "tentative game plan" of waves growing with each roughly two-yearly launch opportunity: five ships in the Mars window opening in late 2026, then 20 in 2028 to 2029, 100 in 2030 to 2031 and 500 in 2033.

facts.label: The 50-50 caveat
facts.value: In the same presentation, Musk put the odds of making the late-2026 window at "50-50", conditional on demonstrating orbital propellant transfer: "We'll try to make that opportunity if we get lucky."

facts.label: SpaceX's 2026 pivot
facts.value: On 8 February 2026 Musk posted that SpaceX "has already shifted focus to building a self-growing city on the Moon, as we can potentially achieve that in less than 10 years, whereas Mars would take 20+ years", adding that SpaceX "will also strive to build a Mars city and begin doing so in about 5 to 7 years, but the overriding priority is securing the future of civilization and the Moon is faster". The Wall Street Journal had reported on 6 February 2026 that SpaceX had abandoned a 2026 Mars mission in favour of an uncrewed lunar landing as soon as March 2027.

facts.label: The whiplash
facts.value: In January 2025 Musk had written, of a proposal to make Starship propellant on the Moon: "No, we're going straight to Mars. The Moon is a distraction." In 2017 he had said the opposite, that a Moon base was what would get the public fired up.

facts.label: Starship status
facts.value: As of the SpaceX earnings call on 4 August 2026, Starship had flown thirteen integrated flight tests and had not yet reached orbit. Flight 13, in July 2026, was suborbital, deployed 20 Starlink V3 satellites that reentered with the ship, and left the ship floating intact in the Indian Ocean. Flight 14 was to be the first attempt to reach orbit with an operational payload. Announced on 4 August 2026 for the end of that month, it slipped into September, and Musk said on 20 August that SpaceX would "probably catch the ship with the tower in a few months" rather than on this flight. After a last slip from 22 September, it flew on 28 September 2026, entered orbit for the first time and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites, then returned early to a controlled splashdown in the Pacific.

facts.label: The missing capability
facts.value: Propellant transfer between two vehicles in space has still not been demonstrated. SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell said on 4 August 2026 that "propellant transfer in orbit is critical to both our internal SpaceX as well as our HLS ambitions". Every Starship Mars architecture depends on refuelling in Earth orbit before departure.

facts.label: Where humans have actually been
facts.value: Artemis II launched on 1 April 2026 and splashed down on 10 April 2026, a mission of 9 days, 1 hour and 32 minutes, carrying four astronauts on a crewed lunar flyby, the first crewed flight beyond low Earth orbit since Apollo 17 in 1972. NASA's own page for the mission describes it as "a key step toward long-term return to the Moon and future missions to Mars". Artemis III, restructured in February 2026 into an Earth-orbit rendezvous and docking test with uncrewed Blue Moon MK2 and Starship HLS articles, is targeted as of September 2026 for 2027; Artemis IV, the intended first landing, for 2028.

facts.label: The nearest thing to a Mars precursor
facts.value: SR-1 Freedom, announced 24 March 2026, is a NASA nuclear electric propulsion demonstrator using a 20 kW HALEU reactor and the power and propulsion element built for the lunar Gateway, which NASA said the same day it intends to pause in its current form. As of September 2026 SR-1 Freedom is targeted to launch in late 2028 with SkyFall aboard and to fly past Mars in 2029. SkyFall, three Ingenuity-class helicopters that would survey candidate human landing sites and look for subsurface water ice, is to land after a second approach to Mars, in autumn 2030; NASA says this timeline will shift as the missions mature. In March 2026 NASA said it had not decided where the mission would end.

facts.label: Cost of the lunar detour
facts.value: NASA's Moon base plan, unveiled at its "Ignition" event on 24 March 2026, runs in three phases over about a decade at roughly $10 billion per phase, and Administrator Jared Isaacman said about $20 billion would be spent over the following seven years. NASA's cost estimate for SR-1 Freedom alone is $2.1 billion, not counting the SkyFall helicopters (Ars Technica, 1 September 2026).

facts.label: What experts say is missing
facts.value: A SpaceNews commentary of 15 July 2026 by Bruce Jakosky, Scott Hubbard, Jennifer Rochlis and Timothy Kokan stated flatly that "we're not yet ready to send people to Mars" and argued that engineering, human health, science and planetary protection must be integrated into one mission design now, before the main hardware is fixed.

facts.label: China
facts.value: China's crewed goal, restated by the China Manned Space Engineering Office on 23 May 2026, is a first Chinese landing on the Moon before 2030; Mars is not in it. Its next Mars mission is robotic: Tianwen-3, which the China National Space Administration said on 24 April 2026 is planned to launch around 2028 and return Martian samples around 2031. A 2009 Chinese Academy of Sciences roadmap forecast that China would have the capability for a crewed Mars landing around 2050, and senior Chinese rocket engineers have named about 2035 as the earliest possible date for a crewed Mars mission, but we found no approved or funded Chinese crewed Mars mission.

facts.label: Dates and time zone
facts.value: Policy documents, speeches and votes here are dated in Washington local time; spaceflight events are dated in UTC. Where a source gives only a month, this entry gives only a month.

timeline: President George H. W. Bush proposes a return to the Moon and then "a manned mission to Mars", with no date attached and the National Space Council asked to come back with costs and realistic timetables. Nothing flew from it.
President Obama tells an audience at Kennedy Space Center that by the mid-2030s humans could orbit Mars, with a landing to follow.

Musk argues for a lunar base: "If you want to get the public really fired up, you've got to have a base on the moon," in a July 2017 speech, and at the International Astronautical Congress, "It's 2017. I mean, we should have a lunar base by now." He will reverse this position twice more.
President Trump's inaugural address promises American astronauts will plant the flag on Mars. No programme or date follows.
Musk, presenting at Starbase, puts the chance of making the late-2026 Mars window at about 50 per cent and makes it conditional on demonstrating orbital propellant transfer.
Executive Order 14369 sets a 2028 crewed lunar return and initial elements of a permanent lunar outpost by 2030, and mentions Mars only as preparation.

The Wall Street Journal reports SpaceX has dropped a 2026 Mars mission in favour of an uncrewed lunar landing as soon as March 2027. Musk then confirms the shift publicly, saying SpaceX would begin building a Mars city "in about 5 to 7 years".

At NASA's "Ignition" event the agency says it intends to pause the lunar Gateway in its current form, and announces both a three-phase Moon base and SR-1 Freedom, a nuclear-electric spacecraft due to launch for Mars in 2028, carrying three small helicopters to scout possible human landing sites.

Artemis II launches on 1 April and splashes down on 10 April, carrying four astronauts around the Moon: the first crewed flight beyond low Earth orbit since 1972, and as of 28 September 2026 the only one.

Four senior Mars figures argue in SpaceNews that "we're not yet ready to send people to Mars" and that the engineering, health, science and planetary-protection work for a human mission must be integrated now.

On its first earnings call as a public company, SpaceX says Starship Flight 14 will attempt orbit and a tower catch of the upper stage. At that point Starship had not yet reached orbit or transferred propellant between two vehicles in space.

Administrator Jared Isaacman says he is "extremely confident" Artemis III will launch in 2027 as an Earth-orbit docking test, with the first lunar landing on Artemis IV in 2028. No NASA official states a human Mars date.

A presidential memorandum on space transportation (NSPM-17) directs NASA to "explore commercial architectures for sending humans to the surface of Mars and returning them to Earth". It sets no Mars date.

Starship Flight 14 reaches orbit for the first time and deploys 26 Starlink V3 satellites, then returns early to a controlled splashdown in the Pacific. Propellant transfer between two vehicles has still not been demonstrated.
